title: Project 2 - Cell extrinsic mechanisms influencing MPN clonal evolution
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – PROJECT 2 (Challen) Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are characterized by overproduction of one or more blood cell types such as red blood cells or platelets. There are more than 300,000 MPN patients in the United States, and due to discrepancies between onset and diagnosis, this estimate is likely low. The most feared complication of MPN is disease progression to secondary acute myeloid leukemia (sAML). sAML patients have no dedicated therapies, leading to extremely poor prognosis with average survival time of six months. Evolution of sAML from MPN is driven by acquisition of additional genetic mutations. The JAK2V617F mutation causes MPN in the majority of patients, but in a substantial proportion of cases, this mutation disappears when they develop sAML. We hypothesize that in these cases, the sAML is caused by a different clone that is nurtured by the JAK2V617F MPN cells. We have preliminary data that supports this model using single cell DNA sequencing to identify which cells carry different mutations. Interestingly, our single cell sequencing results also show that in certain patients this disease evolution can also occur when the JAK2 mutation is sustained. This is because JAK2 mutations in MPN patients can occur in the heterozygous (only one allele of the gene affected) or homozygous (both alleles of the gene affected) state. This makes the clonal organization of the disease in these patients very difficult to understand through traditional genome sequencing approaches used in the clinic. Our data show that both mutation states can occur in the same patient in different cells, and that other mutations that drive the sAML are found in completely separate clones. We hypothesize that these distinct disease entities (MPN vs sAML) in the same patient arise from independent clones derived from a natural history of clonal hematopoiesis (CH), with clinical manifestation of the JAK2-mutant MPN arising before JAK2 wild-type sAML. It is well-described that JAK2V617F cells induce chronic inflammation and we hypothesize that certain cytokines secreted by JAK2V617F MPNs act on independent clones with pathogenic mutations to support their outgrowth in parallel to the MPN disease. We will examine this through the following Specific Aims; • Determine if human MPN cells generate an environment that selects for independent pathogenic clones. • Inhibit cytokines secreted by MPN cells to mitigate expansion of independent pathogenic clones. • Define the evolutionary origins of MPN disease progression using single cell proteogenomics. We will use a complementary combination of single cell approaches, novel genetic mouse models and our unique MPN PDX system to rigorously interrogate this hypothesis. Defining the developmental origins of disease progression in MPN patients can facilitate more appropriate treatment decisions for these patients in the hope of improving survival outcomes. Moreover, identification of prognostic genetic and molecular factors regulating these processes may identify new clinical approaches for these patients.

title: Establishing a Wastewater Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Program (wwGISP) for Early Detection of Community-Level Gonorrhea Transmission and Antimicrobial Resistance
text:
Antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) gonorrhea is an increasingly serious public health concern due to rising
resistance to critical antibiotics, including ceftriaxone. The proposed Wastewater Gonococcal Isolate
Surveillance Program (wwGISP) seeks to enhance existing surveillance methods by implementing wastewater-
based genomic monitoring to provide early, real-time detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and associated AMR
mutations. By leveraging advanced laboratory techniques and novel computational analyses, wwGISP aims to
generate timely and actionable insights into gonorrhea transmission dynamics, significantly strengthening
public health responses and preparedness nationwide.

title: Activity Space Exposures, Safety and Physiological Stress, and their Consequences for Adolescent Health
text:
Modified Narrative / Public Health Relevance:
The objectives of this study are to determine the impact of everyday exposures to area-level violence and collective belonging on perceptions of safety, physiological stress, mental health and substance use.  We will also explore whether changes in the extent and impact of adolescents’ routine exposures have occurred in the last decade.

title: Integrative Health Sciences Facility Core
text: The Integrated Health Sciences Facility Core (IHSFC) facilitates multi-directional translational research between mechanistic, toxicological, clinical, and population-based studies to inform the scientific community, public health policy, and education. The IHSFC furthers the mission of the Southwest Environmental Health Sciences Center (SWEHSC) with a focus on the environmental exposures affecting human health that are unique to the arid Southwest environment. The mission of the IHSFC stems from the three SWEHSC research themes: environmental exposures to people in the Southwest, environmental lung disease, and adaptive responses to environmental stressors, which span a number of environmental exposures including organic solvents, metals and metalloids, airborne particulate matter, and UV light exposure. To foster integrated environmental health research, the IHSFC is organized around three operational components. The Implementation Resource for Translational and Human Exposure Research provides strategic advice and resource support to SWEHSC investigators in sampling Southwest human populations and their living environment, communicating research findings with key stakeholders, and in helping investigators navigate translational research barriers. The Data Science Resource provides statistics, bioinformatics, database development and integration, and highperformance computing support and resources to investigators within a model of project partnership. The Inhalation Exposure Resource provides a vital new core facility to conduct inhalation exposure experiments in rodent and cellular models. By combining these three resource areas, the IHSFC provides integrated services and expertise in environmental exposure measurement and modeling, statistical modeling of the relationship between exposure and health outcomes, and mimicking real world exposures in experimental models of disease to understand their mechanistic underpinnings. IHSFC scientists work with investigators from all three SWEHSC research focus groups (RFGs) and Pilot Projects, serve as mentors for Career Development beneficiaries, and work with the Cellular Imaging and Omics Facility Cores to ensure consistent, professional statistics and bioinformatics study design, data management, and connectivity. Finally, the IHSFC collaborates extensively with the Community Engagement Core (CEC) to leverage established relationships with community stakeholders, identify exposures of concern to communities, assess environmental health literacy, and identify effective strategies for communicating research results and environmental risk to the people of Arizona and the Southwest.

title: Function and regulation of epithelial glycosylation
text:
The surfaces of all mammalian cells are covered with glycosylated molecules. We develop chemical biology
methods to study the function of glycosylated molecules and are working to identify genes that regulate the
production of glycosylated molecules. Understanding the regulation and function of glycosylated molecules has
relevance to human physiology, including susceptibility to infectious diseases and to cancer.

title: Cognitive aging in long-term breast cancer survivors
text:
Despite significant progress in understanding cognitive change around the time of breast cancer diagnosis and
treatment, little is known regarding long-term cognitive trajectories and how these might be impacted by a
history of cancer and cancer treatment. The overall goal of this proposal is to collect and analyze cognitive
performance data at developmentally meaningful intervals 5-20 years post-treatment in older cancer survivors
to determine whether cognitive performance remains stable or instead increasingly declines compared to
individuals without a cancer history. We will also examine cognitive trajectories for their association with
differential deficit accumulation in survivors compared to controls. This research is significant and innovative
because little is known about potentially altered cognitive trajectories and the design and methods proposed
will be able to characterize these trajectories and potential association with deficit accumulation.

title: Exclusive liquid repellency enables next-generation phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing
text:
Bacterial infection continues to be a major global health threat that has been exacerbated by the emergence and
unabated spread of antimicrobial-resistance. The goal of this proposal is to develop a new rapid identification and
antimicrobial susceptibility testing platform for clinical isolates utilizing an exclusive liquid repellency-based under-
oil open microfluidic system to ensure 1) prompt coverage of infecting organisms and 2) prevention of overuse of
broad-spectrum antimicrobials.

title: Combined pharmacologic and AAV gene therapy of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency
text:
The overall goal of this proposal is to develop novel strategies involving a drug (DCA)+gene therapy (AAV)
to treat a children’s disease called pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency. Both DCA and AAV have been used
successfully in humans, but not both together. DCA is safe, as is AAV, which is derived from a virus that causes
no known disease in humans, and therefore, their combination is also expected to be safe, and the development
of such a combination therapy for potential treatment and cure of a debilitating human diseases has relevance
to public health.

title: Core B - Biostatistics/Bioinformatics Core
text:
CORE B PROJECT NARRATIVE
The Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core will provide centralized and comprehensive biostatistical and
bioinformatics expertise to facilitate reliable and reproducible data management and sharing to enhance real-
time interaction, data sharing, and cross-pollination among the P01 components. Core B will play a key role in
the P01 throughout all stages, focused on study conceptualization, data collection, data management, data
analysis, proper use of publicly available resources, and reporting. Core B will enforce scientific rigor and
reproducibility throughout all components of the P01 at all stages and educate investigators to fundamentally
understand statistical and bioinformatics standard workflow and methods that are constantly used in the projects.

title: Elucidating the Sexual Cycle of HIV/AIDS-Related Pneumocystis Pneumonia
text:
Project narrative. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PjP) is the most common opportunistic infection in
persons with HIV. Development of new approaches for therapy and prophylaxis of PjP are critically needed
due to the very limited armamentarium available. The echinocandins halt the ability of these fungi to proceed
through sexual replication. Using single cell RNA-Seq, a rigorous validation pipeline, and in vivo proof- of -
concept, we propose to identify additional drug targets in the sexual cycle with the goal of reducing treatment
time and efficacy with a combination of agents.

title: Extracellular matrix in vertebrate hematopoietic stem cell specification
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are a population of tissue-specific stem cells that live in the bone marrow and both continuously regenerate and replenish blood and immune cells during life. HSCs are the therapeutic component of bone marrow transplants. HSCs are born in the developing embryo and we seek to understand the native conditions that produce HSCs in order to help support attempts to generate them in vitro as a resource for transplant therapies, pharmacological investigation, and disease modeling.

title: Imaging and Radiation Shared Resource
text: IMAGING AND RADIATION SHARED RESOURCE: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The Imaging and Radiation Shared Resource (IRSR) provides value to and enhances the mission of the Wilmot Cancer Institute (Wilmot) by offering education and leading edge experimental resources for all Wilmot investigators that undertake developmental preclinical cancer studies using animal models. Brian Marples, PhD (CM), and V. Kaye Thomas, PhD (ZY), lead the IRSR. The IRSR’s goal is to provide access to state-of-the-art tissue imaging and image-targeted irradiation technologies for all Wilmot investigators, including system-appropriate standardization of methodologies to ensure precision and reproducibility among individual investigators and projects, and between investigators, along with in-depth training. Preclinical studies have adopted clinically equivalent experimental approaches that employ animal models and utilize advanced imaging techniques for both validation of the model and as endpoint assays. For example, for all Wilmot investigators, the IRSR creates dose volume histogram-based radiation plans on an animal-by-animal basis that exploit multiple integrated treatment beams, confirming dosimetry, thus delivering the required radiation dose to the tumor-target volume while minimizing exposure to normal tissues. In addition, pairing targeted radiation dose delivery instrumentation with advanced imaging modalities, such as high-resolution, multi-dimensional confocal or multiphoton microscopy, has elevated state-of-the-art irradiators beyond the scope of most independent laboratories. The IRSR maintains advanced imaging equipment to system-appropriate standards, ensures experimental reproducibility of cancer-related studies, and provides the essential radiation dosimetry needed to operate within nationally recommended best-practice treatment guidelines. Overall, these procedures are designed to ensure greater rigor and reproducibility in accordance with the current standards in the field, as adherence to standardization maintains accuracy and consistency for all cross-program collaborations. Moreover, direct linkage between all preclinical models with data collection and analysis allows for pre-publication sharing of investigational improvements and innovations across various projects, thus minimizing duplication of effort. Reproducible animal modeling and imaging services are essential components of preclinical developmental research to identify and develop novel therapeutic strategies or improve existing strategies, as well as to investigate complex tumor biology. The Cancer Microenvironment and Genetics, Epigenetics and Metabolism research programs predominantly use the IRSR, with over 34% of Wilmot investigators utilizing IRSR services and resources since November 2022. Since 2019, the IRSR has supported >75 peer-reviewed publications and more than 36 NIH-funded (nine NCI-funded) grants led by Wilmot members. Moving forward, the IRSR has invested in enhanced microscopy technology (light sheet) in response to user surveys and developed best practices and standard operating procedures that include radiation dose verification across all radiation platforms and investigators to ensure the accuracy of radiation targeting and dosing.

title: Lymphatic Regeneration by Direct Cellular Reprogramming
text:
Lymphedema is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the USA; however, clinical therapies aiming to
grow lymphatic vessels in the body are currently lacking. Recently, we developed innovative technologies for
directly reprogramming somatic cells toward lymphatic endothelial cells (rLECs), bypassing a stem cell stage. In
this proposal, we will develop clinically compatible ETV2 vector and rLECs, and determine the therapeutic effects
of direct delivery of ETV2 gene aor transplantion of rLECs on lymphedema animal models.

title: Lipid Bilayer Remodeling and Protein Intermediates During Membrane Fusion
text:
Protein-mediated membrane fusion is a fundamental process that is essential for biological
functions as wide ranging as gamete fertilization, formation of placenta, synaptic vesicle trafficking,
tissue development, mitochondrial function, and enveloped virus infection. Despite its significance,
relatively little is understood at a mechanistic and structural level regarding how specialized fusion
protein machinery and membranes interact in order to go from a prefusion to activated fusogenic
to the final formation of a fusion pore. Here cryo-electron microscopy and structural mass
spectrometry will be used to study membrane fusion in two biomedically important enveloped
viruses, thus providing new insights into how very different protein machines accomplish similar
physical functions of merging two distinct membranes into one.

title: Assessing Genomic, Regulatory and Transcriptional Variation at Single Nuclei Resolution in the Brains of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
text:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a disorder of the developing brain that affects millions of individuals, however
the underlying changes in the brain remain poorly characterized. We propose to use brain tissue and brain cells
from individuals with ASD and unaffected controls to find differing patterns of gene expression and gene
regulation and perform parallel analyses in a brain organoids grown from stem cells with ASD mutations. By
assessing the overlap with known genetic risk factors and genetic regions that control gene expression, we hope
to provide insights into biology that could be beneficial for developing therapeutics in the future.

title: Resource Core I: Genomic Outcomes Core
text: The mission of “Resource Core I: the Genomic Outcomes Core” is to provide a suite of high-quality turn-key DNA-based assays for monitoring the safety and efficacy of genome editing to support the Correction of Neurological Disease via Allele Specific Excision of Pathogenic Repeats (CASEPR) program. The Genomic Outcomes Core will provide the fundamental role of directly assessing the genomic effects of nuclease-based therapeutic treatment at the target site (including measuring excision efficiency) and off-target regions of the genome, both in cell culture models, and in experimental animal models; as such, the outcomes assessed by the Core will complement the in vivo and biological impacts assessed by Cores II and III, respectively. For each assay the Core will work with the appropriate project team or Core to onboard project-specific reagents or tissues (RNPs, AAVs, cell lines, genomic DNAs etc). Working with the Administrative Core, results from analysis of all the samples will be cataloged within the laboratory information management system (LIMS) and result reports will be provided to the Project Teams via a standardized LIMS interface. These data will enable the selection of preclinical leads, and provide critical feedback on genomic outcomes in cell and animal model systems. Further, data on potency and specificity of genomic outcomes driven by preclinical Cas9-gRNA combinations for all three Research Projects will provide a key basis for study reports to be provided to the FDA as part of regulatory filings to ensure timely progress to IND. From a logistics perspective the consolidation of expertise for genomic assays within the Genomic Outcomes Core will promote rapid and robust input-to-answer solutions for Project Teams across the entire lifespan of all three Research Projects.

title: Vesicle fusion regulation in metabolism
text:
Vesicle fusion – the merging of two separate lipid bilayers into one – is a biological process underlying key
metabolic pathways. Imbalances in metabolic vesicle fusion are associated with metabolic disorders, including
insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Molecular insights acquired from this work will pave the way for developing
new therapeutics for these disorders.

title: UC Berkeley Vision Science CORE
text:
The Core grant provides ongoing support to the vision science research community on the UC
Berkeley campus, engaged in a broad range of research of the eye and visual system - from basic
mechanisms of vision through translation and application of new therapies to people with vision
disorders.

title: Deciphering the Role of Glycan Sulfation in Neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder that affects every 1 in 9 Americans aged 65
and older. Mounting evidence links dysfunctional brain perineuronal nets (PNNs) and their sulfated
glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) as an underlying driver of AD progression through the promotion of neurocircuit
destabilization. The goal of this proposal is to determine novel mechanisms linking changes in brain PNN glycans
sulfation patterning with neuroinflammation and loss of stable PNN matrices inherent to AD, thus providing a
novel foundation upon which new targets and therapies for AD can be developed and tested.

title: Neural mechanisms of social attachment disruption in frontotemporal dementia
text:
Neurodegenerative disease incidence is increasing as our population ages, yet we lack effective treatments for
these diseases. While the social behavior changes that occur across many dementias, particularly
frontotemporal dementia (FTD), account for a tremendous portion of disease burden, these behavioral sequelae
have been understudied as a mechanistic entity or therapeutic target. The proposed project will develop a novel
animal model to examine the genetic, molecular, and neural circuit factors that underlie social attachment deficits
in FTD and other neurodegenerative diseases.
